walkthrough:
What a Plasmid Is - The Basic Structure**
Think of a plasmid sitting beside me as a tiny extra loop of DNA in the cytoplasm of a bacterium. It is double-stranded DNA, just like the chromosome, but it is very small and circular. Small means it can easily enter a host cell during transformation, and circular means it has no free ends so it is stable and less easily broken down.

Opening It Up - Restriction Sites**
To use it as a vector you need a place to put your gene. Plasmids used in cloning have restriction sites, which are specific target sequences for restriction enzymes. Cutting there opens the circle at one controlled point so the desired gene can be inserted without disrupting essential plasmid functions.

Finding the Transformed Cells - Marker Genes**
A common confusion is thinking all bacteria take up the plasmid. In reality only a few do. That is why plasmids carry marker genes, typically genes for antibiotic resistance. Only bacteria that have taken up the plasmid will survive on antibiotic plates, so you can identify the GM / transformed / recombinant cells.

Making Many Copies - Independent Replication**
Finally, remember plasmids replicate independently of the main bacterial chromosome and often very fast. That means once inside, one plasmid with your inserted gene is copied again and again as the bacterium divides, giving many copies of the cloned gene from one original insertion.

Final answer: Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that are stable. They have restriction sites / target sequences for restriction enzymes allowing the gene for cloning to be inserted. They can enter / transform host bacterial cells. They contain marker genes such as antibiotic resistance genes used to identify transformed / recombinant cells. They replicate independently and rapidly of host replication to give many copies of the cloned gene.

walkthrough:
Restriction Endonucleases - The Molecular Scissors**
These enzymes do not cut randomly. They recognise and cut DNA at a specific base sequence called a restriction site, often a palindrome where the sequence reads the same on both strands. Depending on where they cut they leave sticky ends with single-stranded overhangs or blunt ends with no overhangs. You use the same enzyme on both the donor DNA and the plasmid so the ends match.

DNA Ligase - The Molecular Glue**
Cutting and lining up the gene next to the opened plasmid is not enough because the sugar-phosphate backbone is still broken. Ligase joins the gene to the plasmid / vector by sealing that backbone. It catalyses formation of phosphodiester covalent bonds between adjacent nucleotides, creating a continuous recombinant DNA / recombinant plasmid molecule.

Reverse Transcriptase - From mRNA Back to DNA**
Sometimes you want only the expressed part of a eukaryotic gene with no introns. You start with mRNA and use reverse transcriptase, which does the reverse of transcription. It uses mRNA as a template to make single-stranded cDNA first, which is then made double-stranded. This cDNA can then be cut with restriction enzymes and ligated into a vector as above.

Putting the Story Together**
So the flow is logical: reverse transcriptase provides intron-free cDNA if needed, restriction endonuclease cuts both gene and vector to give compatible ends, and ligase seals them into recombinant DNA ready for cloning in plasmids.

Final answer: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at restriction sites / specific base sequences / palindromic sequences to give sticky or blunt ends. DNA ligase joins the gene to the plasmid / vector by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone, forming phosphodiester / covalent bonds to make recombinant DNA / plasmid. Reverse transcriptase makes single-stranded then double-stranded cDNA from an mRNA template.
